topics.title: Introduction to React
topics.content: React is a JavaScript library built by Facebook for making user interfaces. Instead of reloading the whole page, React updates only the parts of the screen that change.
topics.definition: React is a JavaScript library for building reusable UI components and updating the browser efficiently.
topics.why: React helps build complex interfaces by managing UI state and updating only what changes instead of reloading the whole page.
topics.problem: Without React, managing interactive UI state requires manual DOM updates, which is error-prone and slow for larger applications.
topics.realWorldExample: A dashboard that refreshes only the chart widgets when new data arrives instead of re-rendering the entire page.
topics.commonMistakes: Mutating component state directly and using array indexes as keys can cause rendering bugs.

questions.question: What is React?
questions.answer: React is an open-source JavaScript library for building single-page user interfaces using components.

questions.question: What is the Virtual DOM?
questions.answer: It is an in-memory representation of the real DOM that React keeps in sync to optimize rendering speed.

topics.title: JSX (JavaScript XML)
topics.content: JSX stands for JavaScript XML. It lets you write HTML-like code directly inside your JavaScript. To write dynamic values inside JSX, wrap any valid JavaScript expression in curly braces `{}`. This combines structural layout with JavaScript logic.

questions.question: What does JSX stand for?
questions.answer: JSX stands for JavaScript XML.

questions.question: Why do we use curly braces in JSX?
questions.answer: To evaluate JavaScript expressions, variables, or function calls directly inside JSX.

topics.definition: JSX is a syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript code.
topics.why: It makes React components easier to read and write by looking similar to the UI they create.
topics.problem: Without JSX, building a React component would require nested function calls and less readable code.
topics.realWorldExample:
Using JSX lets you return
Hello
directly from a React component.
topics.commonMistakes: Forgetting to close tags or using JavaScript expressions outside of { } are common JSX errors.

topics.title: Components
topics.content: Components are the self-contained building blocks of a React app. They are simple JavaScript functions that return JSX. By splitting your page into smaller components (like a Header, Button, or Card), you can reuse and test code easily.

questions.question: What is a component in React?
questions.answer: A component is a modular, reusable function that returns JSX and describes a piece of the UI.

questions.question: What are the rules of naming React components?
questions.answer: React component names must always start with a capital letter (e.g. Header, not header).

topics.definition: Components are reusable pieces of UI in React that usually return JSX.
topics.why: They help you break a page into smaller, easier-to-manage parts.
topics.problem: Without components, large apps become hard to organize and hard to reuse.
topics.realWorldExample: A header, footer, and card can all be separate components reused across pages.
topics.commonMistakes: Making components too large or putting unrelated logic in one component makes maintenance harder.

topics.title: Props
topics.content: Props (short for properties) are inputs you pass from a parent component down to a child component, just like arguments in a function. Props are read-only (immutable)—a component must never modify its own props.

questions.question: What are props in React?
questions.answer: Props are read-only properties passed from parent components to child components.

questions.question: Can a child component update its own props?
questions.answer: No, props are read-only and should never be modified inside the child component.

topics.definition: Props are values passed from a parent component to a child component.
topics.why: They allow components to work with different data without changing their internal code.
topics.problem: Props solve the need to customize a child component from the outside.
topics.realWorldExample: Passing a user name into a greeting component so it can show Hello, Ashutosh.
topics.commonMistakes: Trying to change props inside a child component or missing required props are common mistakes.

topics.title: useState
topics.content: State is data inside a component that can change over time (like a form input or a counter). The `useState` hook allows functional components to have state. It returns two items: the current state value, and a function to update it.

questions.question: What is state in React?
questions.answer: State is dynamic data managed internally by a component that can change and trigger a re-render.

questions.question: What does the useState hook return?
questions.answer: An array containing the current state value and a setter function to update that value.

topics.definition: useState lets a React component hold local data that can change over time.
topics.why: It updates the UI automatically when the state changes.
topics.problem: Without state, your UI cannot react to user input or dynamic values.
topics.realWorldExample: A counter button that updates the number each time it is clicked.
topics.commonMistakes: Directly modifying state or using the wrong state variable in the update function can cause bugs.

topics.title: Event Handling
topics.content: React handles events like clicks, form submissions, and text typing using camelCase attributes (like `onClick` or `onChange`) rather than lowercase. You pass function references directly to these event handlers.

questions.question: How do you handle click events in React?
questions.answer: Pass a function reference to the onClick attribute of an element, e.g. onClick={myFunction}.

questions.question: How is React event handling different from standard HTML?
questions.answer: React uses camelCase naming (onClick) and passes function objects instead of string actions.

topics.definition: Event handling in React lets components respond to user actions like clicks and typing.
topics.why: It makes your app interactive and able to react to user input.
topics.problem: Without event handlers, buttons and forms would not do anything when clicked or submitted.
topics.realWorldExample: Showing an alert when a user clicks a button.
topics.commonMistakes: Calling the handler instead of passing it as a reference or using the wrong event property are common errors.

topics.title: Conditional Rendering
topics.content: Conditional rendering allows you to display different UI layouts depending on conditions (like checking if a user is logged in). You can do this using standard JavaScript `if` statements, ternary operators `? :`, or the logical logical-AND `&&` operator.

questions.question: How can you conditionally render JSX?
questions.answer: Use the ternary operator (? :), logical AND (&&), or simple if-else statements.

questions.question: What does double ampersand (&&) do in JSX?
questions.answer: It renders the element on the right only if the condition on the left evaluates to true.

topics.definition: Conditional rendering shows or hides parts of the UI based on a condition.
topics.why: It lets you display different content for different app states.
topics.problem: Without it, you cannot show login screens, loading messages, or error states correctly.
topics.realWorldExample: Display a welcome message only when the user is logged in.
topics.commonMistakes: Using && incorrectly with falsy values or not handling the else case can cause unexpected output.

topics.title: Lists and Keys
topics.content: When rendering arrays of data in JSX, we use the `.map()` method to loop over elements. Each item in the loop needs a unique `key` prop. Keys help React identify which items have changed, been added, or been removed, optimizing performance.

questions.question: Why do list items need a unique key prop?
questions.answer: Keys help React track which items changed, added, or removed for efficient rendering.

questions.question: Should you use index numbers as keys?
questions.answer: Only as a last resort. If the list can change order, using index can cause rendering bugs and slowdowns.

topics.definition: Lists and keys are used to render arrays of elements efficiently in React.
topics.why: Keys help React track items when the list changes, so updates stay fast and correct.
topics.problem: Without unique keys, React may reuse the wrong DOM elements when a list changes.
topics.realWorldExample: Rendering a list of products, each with a unique key from its id.
topics.commonMistakes: Using array indexes as keys when the list can change order may cause bugs.

topics.title: Controlled vs. Uncontrolled Components
topics.content: In React, form inputs can be managed in two ways. Controlled inputs store their value in React state and update via `onChange`. Uncontrolled inputs let the browser handle the form state directly, and you query the values when needed using a `useRef` hook.

questions.question: What is a controlled component?
questions.answer: An input element whose value is controlled by React state and updated via state setter functions.

questions.question: What is an uncontrolled component?
questions.answer: An input element whose value is managed by the DOM and accessed using refs rather than React state.

topics.definition: Controlled components store their form values in React state, while uncontrolled components rely on the browser DOM.
topics.why: Controlled components give you full control over form input values in React.
topics.problem: Uncontrolled inputs make it harder to validate or update values programmatically.
topics.realWorldExample: A controlled text input updates state on each keystroke and renders the current value.
topics.commonMistakes: Mixing controlled and uncontrolled inputs or forgetting the onChange handler causes warnings.

topics.title: useEffect
topics.content: The `useEffect` hook lets you synchronize a component with external systems (performing side effects like fetching database data, timers, or custom DOM updates). It runs after the component renders. It takes a second argument: a dependency array of variables. The hook re-runs only when these variables change.

questions.question: What does useEffect do?
questions.answer: It runs side effects (e.g. data fetching, event listeners) after the component renders.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the dependency array in useEffect?
questions.answer: It controls when the hook runs. If variables in the array change, the effect runs again.

topics.definition: useEffect runs side effects after a component renders, such as fetching data or setting up timers.
topics.why: It lets React perform tasks that are not part of rendering the UI.
topics.problem: Without useEffect, side effects would run in the render flow and cause bugs or repeated calls.
topics.realWorldExample: Loading user data from an API when the component first appears.
topics.commonMistakes: Forgetting the dependency array or using stale values inside the effect can lead to bugs.

topics.title: useReducer
topics.content: The `useReducer` hook is used for managing complex state logic across multiple actions (like a shopping cart or multi-step checkout form). It works like Redux: you create a `reducer` function that takes the current state and an `action` and returns a brand-new state.

questions.question: When should you use useReducer instead of useState?
questions.answer: When you have complex state transitions, related state values, or want to decouple state updates from UI logic.

questions.question: What are actions and dispatch in useReducer?
questions.answer: An action describes what occurred, and dispatch is the function used to trigger the action in the reducer.

topics.definition: useReducer manages complex component state using a reducer function and actions.
topics.why: It keeps state updates predictable when many values or actions are involved.
topics.problem: Without useReducer, complex state logic can become hard to manage with useState.
topics.realWorldExample: A shopping cart where adding, removing, and clearing items are handled by actions.
topics.commonMistakes: Mutating state directly inside the reducer or using inconsistent action shapes are common issues.

topics.title: useContext
topics.content: Context provides a way to pass data through the component tree without having to pass props down manually at every level (known as prop drilling). The `useContext` hook lets you subscribe to global variables, like a user profile status or styling themes.

questions.question: What is prop drilling?
questions.answer: Prop drilling is the process of passing props through intermediate components that do not need the data, just to reach a deep child.

questions.question: What does useContext solve?
questions.answer: It provides a global data channel to share state directly with deep children, eliminating prop drilling.

topics.definition: useContext allows components to access shared data without passing props through every level.
topics.why: It simplifies prop passing for data like themes, user info, or settings.
topics.problem: Without context, you might need deep prop drilling across many components.
topics.realWorldExample: Using a ThemeContext to let any component read the current light or dark theme.
topics.commonMistakes: Reading the wrong context provider or not wrapping components in the provider causes undefined values.

topics.title: useRef
topics.content: The `useRef` hook lets you create a reference to a DOM node directly (for focusing inputs, playing media, or measuring layout sizes) or to store a value that persists between renders without triggering a re-render when it changes.

questions.question: What are the two main use cases of useRef?
questions.answer: To hold direct references to DOM elements, and to store mutable values that persist across renders without triggering page updates.

questions.question: Does updating ref.current trigger a component re-render?
questions.answer: No, mutating current ref values does not trigger re-rendering.

topics.definition: useRef stores a mutable reference that persists across renders without causing re-renders.
topics.why: It is useful for accessing DOM elements or keeping a value between renders.
topics.problem: Without useRef, you would lose a value after every component render or cause extra updates.
topics.realWorldExample: Focusing an input element automatically when the page loads.
topics.commonMistakes: Expecting ref.current to update instantly or using refs for state-like values can be confusing.

topics.title: useMemo & useCallback
topics.content: These are optimization hooks. `useMemo` caches (memoizes) the *result* of a slow calculation, so it doesn't run again unless dependencies change. `useCallback` caches the *function definition* itself, preventing React from recreating it on every single render.

questions.question: What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback?
questions.answer: useMemo caches the returned value of a calculation, whereas useCallback caches the function definition itself.

questions.question: Should you wrap all functions in useCallback?
questions.answer: No, optimization hooks have overhead. Use them only when passing functions to memoized child components to prevent unnecessary updates.

topics.definition: useMemo and useCallback help React avoid re-running expensive calculations or re-creating functions unnecessarily.
topics.why: They improve performance by stabilizing values and functions across renders.
topics.problem: Without them, expensive work may run on every render and slow the app down.
topics.realWorldExample: Memoizing a filtered list or a click handler so it does not change unless inputs change.
topics.commonMistakes: Overusing memoization when it is not needed adds complexity without performance benefit.

topics.title: Custom Hooks
topics.content: Custom hooks let you extract component logic into reusable functions. If two or more components need to perform the same action (like checking online status or fetching API data), you can create a custom function starting with `use` (e.g. `useOnlineStatus`) that wraps existing React hooks.

questions.question: What is a custom hook in React?
questions.answer: A custom hook is a reusable JavaScript function starting with 'use' that calls other hooks to bundle shared logic.

questions.question: Do custom hooks share state between components?
questions.answer: No, each component that calls a custom hook gets its own isolated, independent state.

topics.definition: Custom hooks are reusable functions that use React hooks and share common logic across components.
topics.why: They avoid duplicating hook logic and keep components cleaner.
topics.problem: Without custom hooks, repeated logic can make components larger and harder to maintain.
topics.realWorldExample: A useFetch hook that fetches data, handles loading, and returns the result.
topics.commonMistakes: Calling hooks conditionally or not following hook naming rules breaks React rules of hooks.

topics.title: Error Boundaries
topics.content: An Error Boundary is a special component that catches JavaScript errors anywhere in its child component tree, logs those errors, and displays a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole webpage. Currently, error boundaries must be class components using lifecycle methods.

questions.question: What is an Error Boundary?
questions.answer: A component that catches JavaScript errors in its child components and renders a fallback UI instead of crashing the application.

questions.question: Can functional components be Error Boundaries?
questions.answer: No, functional components cannot currently implement lifecycle methods like componentDidCatch.

topics.definition: Error boundaries catch JavaScript errors in a part of the UI and show a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app.
topics.why: They keep your app running when one component fails unexpectedly.
topics.problem: Without error boundaries, a rendering error can make the entire React tree disappear.
topics.realWorldExample: Showing a friendly error message for a broken widget while the rest of the page still works.
topics.commonMistakes: Using error boundaries for data fetching errors rather than render-time exceptions is a common misuse.

topics.title: React Router (Routing)
topics.content: React is built for single-page applications (SPAs), meaning it doesn't reload pages from the server. React Router is the standard library used to switch between different page views (like `/about` or `/profile`) client-side without page refreshes.

questions.question: What is the purpose of React Router?
questions.answer: To enable dynamic, client-side routing and page transitions in Single Page Applications.

questions.question: What is the difference between Link and a traditional anchor tag?
questions.answer: Link changes the URL client-side using history state, preventing a full page refresh.

topics.definition: React Router manages navigation and multiple pages inside a React single-page app.
topics.why: It lets you show different views based on the URL without reloading the page.
topics.problem: Without routing, every navigation would require a full page refresh or manual view switching.
topics.realWorldExample: Switching between home, about, and profile screens inside a React app.
topics.commonMistakes: Forgetting to wrap routes in BrowserRouter or using incorrect path matching can break navigation.

topics.title: React Portals
topics.content: Portals let you render a component's JSX outside its parent DOM element, directly into another spot in the HTML tree (like the end of `<body>`). This is incredibly useful for overlays, tooltips, dialogs, or modals that require escaping parent containers.

questions.question: What are React Portals?
questions.answer: A way to render components into a DOM node that exists outside the main React parent container hierarchy.

questions.question: When should you use a Portal?
questions.answer: For UI elements that need to escape parent CSS container restrictions, such as modals, tooltips, and dropdowns.

topics.definition: Portals let you render a component’s children into a DOM node outside the main React tree.
topics.why: They are useful for overlays, modals, and tooltips that should appear above other content.
topics.problem: Without portals, positioning modals and overlays correctly can be difficult inside nested containers.
topics.realWorldExample: Rendering a modal window into a root-level div while keeping the modal logic inside React.
topics.commonMistakes: Forgetting to provide the target DOM node or using portals for normal layout content is not ideal.

topics.title: Suspense & Lazy Loading
topics.content: Lazy loading helps you split your javascript bundle into smaller chunks that load only when needed. You declare components dynamically using `React.lazy()`, and wrap them in a `<Suspense>` component which displays a fallback UI (like a loading spinner) while the bundle downloads.

questions.question: What is code splitting?
questions.answer: Breaking a large JavaScript bundle into smaller files loaded dynamically to improve initial load speed.

questions.question: What does the Suspense component do?
questions.answer: Suspense displays a loading or fallback UI until its dynamically imported child components are ready to render.

topics.definition: Suspense and lazy loading delay loading parts of the app until they are needed.
topics.why: They make apps load faster by splitting code and loading only what is required now.
topics.problem: Without lazy loading, the entire app can become slow to load on first visit.
topics.realWorldExample: Loading a dashboard widget only when the user navigates to the dashboard page.
topics.commonMistakes: Not wrapping lazy components in a Suspense fallback causes errors during loading.

topics.title: React Strict Mode
topics.content: StrictMode is a helper component that activates checks and warnings during development. It helps uncover potential bugs, deprecations, and side-effects. In development mode, StrictMode renders components twice to detect state mutations and clean up issues with lifecycle events.

questions.question: What is the purpose of React.StrictMode?
questions.answer: To highlight potential code problems, memory leaks, and legacy APIs in development mode.

questions.question: Why do my useEffect hooks run twice in React development?
questions.answer: React Strict Mode runs mounts and unmounts twice in dev mode to help you identify missing cleanup functions.

topics.definition: React Strict Mode helps find unsafe or deprecated code by running extra checks during development.
topics.why: It catches problems early before they become bugs in production.
topics.problem: Without Strict Mode, some broken patterns may remain unnoticed until later.
topics.realWorldExample: Wrapping the app in <React.StrictMode> during development to see warnings.
topics.commonMistakes: Expecting Strict Mode to change production behavior; it only runs extra checks in development.

topics.title: Forms and Validation
topics.content: In React, form data is typically handled by components using state (controlled components). Standard validation involves checking the state values before submission. For large forms, packages like React Hook Form or Formik are used to manage complex validation, errors, and rendering behavior efficiently without unnecessary re-renders.

questions.question: What is the recommended way to handle forms in React?
questions.answer: Using controlled components where input values are bound to state and updated via onChange handlers. For very complex forms, libraries like React Hook Form are recommended.

questions.question: How do you prevent a form from reloading the browser page on submit?
questions.answer: By calling e.preventDefault() inside the form's onSubmit event handler.

topics.definition: Forms in React let users submit data through inputs, checkboxes, and buttons.
topics.why: They are the standard way to gather user input in an app.
topics.problem: Without forms, users cannot enter and submit data safely in a React app.
topics.realWorldExample: A login form that captures email and password and submits them to a server.
topics.commonMistakes: Not preventing default form submission or not validating input are common form bugs.

topics.title: State Management
topics.content: As applications grow, passing state down through props (prop drilling) becomes difficult. While React Context is great for static global data (like themes), high-frequency state updates can trigger unnecessary renders. External state libraries like Redux Toolkit or Zustand provide centralized stores with selectors, optimizing rendering performance and decoupling business logic from UI components.

questions.question: When should you use Redux or Zustand instead of Context API?
questions.answer: Use them when you have complex state logic, frequent state updates, or want optimized rendering where components only re-render when their specific selected state changes.

questions.question: What is selector-based state fetching in Zustand/Redux?
questions.answer: It allows a component to subscribe only to a specific slice of state, avoiding re-renders when other unrelated state slices update.

topics.definition: State management is the process of keeping app data organized and in sync with the UI.
topics.why: It ensures that the UI reflects the current app state correctly.
topics.problem: Poor state management leads to confusing or inconsistent screens.
topics.realWorldExample: Keeping track of whether a user is logged in and showing the right menu items.
topics.commonMistakes: Putting too much state in one component or using props to pass data too deeply are common issues.

topics.title: Data Fetching and Caching
topics.content: Data fetching is a side effect often handled inside a useEffect hook. However, manual fetching requires managing loading, error, and cached states. Libraries like TanStack Query (React Query) automate this by caching server data, syncing updates, refetching on window focus, and managing queries and mutations seamlessly.

questions.question: What are the drawbacks of fetching data inside useEffect?
questions.answer: You have to manually write code for loading states, error handling, caching, request de-duplication, and refetching on updates.

questions.question: What is the benefit of TanStack Query?
questions.answer: It automatically caches API requests, handles loading and error states, background updates, and minimizes duplicate network requests.

topics.definition: Data fetching is loading information from an API and displaying it in the app.
topics.why: Most apps need data from servers to show current content or user information.
topics.problem: Without fetching, the app cannot use live data or update based on server changes.
topics.realWorldExample: Loading a list of posts from an API when a page first opens.
topics.commonMistakes: Not handling loading and error states or repeating fetch calls on every render are common mistakes.

topics.title: Styling in React
topics.content: React supports multiple styling approaches. Inline styles use JavaScript objects. Standard CSS is global. CSS Modules scope CSS classes locally to prevent class name clashes. CSS-in-JS (like Styled Components) lets you write CSS inside components using tag template literals, making styles dynamic based on props.

questions.question: What is a CSS Module?
questions.answer: A CSS file where all class names are scoped locally to the component importing them, preventing class name collisions.

questions.question: What are Styled Components?
questions.answer: A CSS-in-JS library that allows you to write CSS syntax directly inside JS/TS files, creating components styled dynamically with props.

topics.definition: Styling controls how a React app looks using CSS, inline styles, or styled components.
topics.why: Good styling makes your app easier to use and more visually appealing.
topics.problem: Without styling, the UI looks plain and hard to read.
topics.realWorldExample: Changing a button color based on whether it is active or disabled.
topics.commonMistakes: Using class instead of className or mixing styles inconsistently can cause layout issues.

topics.title: Testing React Components
topics.content: React components are tested using unit and integration testing frameworks. Vitest (or Jest) is the test runner, while React Testing Library (RTL) provides utilities to render components and query the DOM. RTL encourages testing components from the user's perspective rather than internal state details.

questions.question: Why is React Testing Library preferred over Enzyme?
questions.answer: RTL tests components by interacting with the DOM like a real user, rather than testing component internals, leading to more resilient tests.

questions.question: What is screen in React Testing Library?
questions.answer: An object that provides pre-bound queries to search the entire rendered DOM for specific elements.

topics.definition: Testing checks that React components work correctly and keep working after changes.
topics.why: It prevents bugs and makes refactoring safer.
topics.problem: Without tests, small changes can accidentally break existing functionality.
topics.realWorldExample: Checking that a button click updates the screen as expected.
topics.commonMistakes: Testing implementation details instead of user-visible behavior makes tests fragile.

topics.title: React 18/19 & Server Components
topics.content: React 18 introduced Concurrent Rendering, useTransition, and useDeferredValue to keep UIs responsive during expensive updates. React 19 builds on this with Server Components (RSC), which run exclusively on the server to reduce bundle sizes and improve loading speeds, alongside Actions for simpler form submissions and state sync.

questions.question: What are React Server Components (RSC)?
questions.answer: Components that run and render on the server, sending zero client-side JavaScript to the browser for faster initial page loads.

questions.question: What does useTransition do in React 18/19?
questions.answer: It allows you to mark state updates as non-blocking transitions, keeping the user interface responsive during slow operations.

topics.definition: React 18 and 19 include modern features like automatic batching and improved streaming rendering.
topics.why: They make React apps faster and more responsive with better support for server rendering.
topics.problem: Older versions can feel slower and harder to scale for modern UI patterns.
topics.realWorldExample: Rendering pages on the server and hydrating them on the client for faster load times.
topics.commonMistakes: Expecting all new behavior in production without reading the upgrade guide may cause surprises.

topics.title: Dot Net Overview
topics.content: The .NET platform is a developer platform for building many types of applications. It supports languages like C#, F#, and Visual Basic.
topics.example:
using System;
class Program { static void Main() { Console.WriteLine("Hello from .NET"); } }

questions.question: What is .NET?
questions.answer: .NET is a free, cross-platform, open source developer platform for building many types of applications.

topics.definition: .NET is a framework for building applications using languages like C# and F#.
topics.why: It gives you tools for web, desktop, mobile, and cloud apps with a shared runtime.
topics.problem: Without .NET, you would need different stacks for each platform and less shared code.
topics.realWorldExample: Building a web API and a console app using the same .NET libraries.
topics.practicalExample:
using System;
class Program { static void Main() { Console.WriteLine("Hello from .NET"); } }
topics.commonMistakes: Not understanding the difference between .NET runtime and language features can be confusing.

topics.title: Runtime and Framework
topics.content: The .NET runtime executes managed code and includes services like garbage collection and assembly loading.
topics.example: // .NET code compiled to IL runs on the CLR runtime.

questions.question: What is the CLR in .NET?
questions.answer: The CLR is the Common Language Runtime that executes managed .NET code and provides services such as garbage collection.

topics.definition: The .NET runtime is the engine that executes .NET programs on different operating systems.
topics.why: It allows the same .NET app to run on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
topics.problem: Without a runtime, compiled .NET code could not execute consistently across platforms.
topics.realWorldExample: Running the same web service on a Windows server and a Linux container.
topics.practicalExample: // .NET code compiled to IL runs on the CLR runtime.
topics.commonMistakes: Mixing runtime-specific libraries or assuming Windows-only behavior can break cross-platform apps.

topics.title: Dependency Injection
topics.content:
.NET has built-in support for Dependency Injection (DI). DI is a design pattern that achieves Inversion of Control (IoC) between classes and their dependencies. Services can be registered with three lifetimes:
1. **Transient**: Created each time they are requested.
2. **Scoped**: Created once per client request (e.g. per HTTP request in a web app).
3. **Singleton**: Created once and shared globally.

questions.question: What is the difference between Scoped and Transient service lifetimes?
questions.answer: Transient services are instantiated every time they are requested, while Scoped services are instantiated once per client request (e.g., HTTP request).

questions.question: Can you inject a Scoped service into a Singleton service?
questions.answer: No, doing so causes a captive dependency error because the Scoped service would be kept alive as a Singleton, violating its lifetime scope.

topics.definition: Dependency injection passes needed services into classes instead of creating them directly.
topics.why: It makes code easier to test and swap out implementations.
topics.problem: Without DI, classes become tightly coupled and hard to change.
topics.realWorldExample: Injecting a database service into a controller instead of new-ing it inside the controller.
topics.commonMistakes: Registering the wrong service lifetime or forgetting to register a dependency causes runtime failures.

topics.title: LINQ (Language Integrated Query)
topics.content: LINQ provides a uniform way to query data from collections, databases, and XML files. It supports two syntaxes: Query Syntax (SQL-like) and Method Syntax (using lambda expressions). LINQ utilizes Deferred Execution, meaning queries are not executed when defined, but rather when they are iterated over (e.g., in a foreach loop or by calling ToList()).

questions.question: What is deferred execution in LINQ?
questions.answer: Deferred execution means the query is not evaluated when created, but only when the results are actually iterated or converted (e.g., via ToList()).

questions.question: What is the difference between IEnumerable and IQueryable?
questions.answer: IEnumerable queries in-memory collections client-side, while IQueryable parses expression trees to execute queries directly on databases.

topics.definition: LINQ is a way to query collections and data using readable operators inside C#.
topics.why: It makes filtering, sorting, and searching data simpler and more expressive.
topics.problem: Without LINQ, data manipulation requires more manual loops and boilerplate code.
topics.realWorldExample: Selecting users with ages over 18 from a list of user objects.
topics.commonMistakes: Using query syntax and method syntax inconsistently or forcing immediate execution can cause unexpected behavior.

topics.title: Entity Framework Core (EF Core)
topics.content: EF Core is a lightweight, cross-platform Object-Relational Mapper (ORM) for .NET. It lets you interact with databases using C# objects. The `DbContext` class coordinates EF database operations, tracking changes so they can be persisted via `SaveChanges()`. You use Code-First Migrations to keep the database schema in sync with your C# models.

questions.question: What is the difference between code-first and database-first in EF Core?
questions.answer: Code-first creates database tables from C# classes via migrations, while database-first generates C# classes from an existing database schema.

questions.question: Why should you use AsNoTracking() in EF Core queries?
questions.answer: To improve performance in read-only queries by telling EF Core not to track entity state changes in memory.

topics.definition: EF Core is a .NET library that maps database tables to C# classes for easier data access.
topics.why: It saves time by letting you work with objects instead of raw SQL queries.
topics.problem: Without EF Core, database code becomes repetitive and harder to maintain.
topics.realWorldExample: Loading products from a database into a list of Product objects.
topics.commonMistakes: Ignoring change tracking or using lazy loading without understanding it can lead to performance issues.

topics.title: Asynchronous Programming (async/await)
topics.content: Asynchronous programming in .NET uses `async` and `await` keywords with `Task` objects to write non-blocking code. This prevents threads from being blocked during long operations (like database or network calls), letting the application scale and handle more concurrent requests.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Task class in C#?
questions.answer: A Task represents an ongoing, asynchronous operation that will yield a result in the future.

questions.question: What is the difference between Task.Run and async/await?
questions.answer: Task.Run queues work on a separate ThreadPool thread, while async/await uses non-blocking callbacks for I/O bound operations.

topics.definition: Async programming lets .NET apps run tasks without blocking the main thread.
topics.why: It keeps applications responsive while waiting for I/O like web requests or database calls.
topics.problem: Without async, long-running work would freeze the app or server thread.
topics.realWorldExample: Calling a web API with await instead of blocking the thread until the response arrives.
topics.commonMistakes: Using async without await or returning void from async methods can cause subtle bugs.

topics.title: Memory Management & GC
topics.content: .NET uses automatic memory management handled by the Garbage Collector (GC). The GC allocates and releases memory for managed objects on the heap. Heap objects are split into three generations (Gen 0 for short-lived, Gen 1, and Gen 2 for long-lived objects). Unmanaged resources (like files, databases, network sockets) must be manually released using the `IDisposable` interface and `using` statements.

questions.question: How do the three generations (Gen 0, 1, 2) work in the .NET GC?
questions.answer: Gen 0 holds new short-lived objects. Gen 1 is a buffer zone. Gen 2 holds long-lived objects. Objects surviving collections are promoted to the next generation.

questions.question: Why is the IDisposable interface important?
questions.answer: It provides a standard way to release unmanaged resources immediately without waiting for the Garbage Collector to run.

topics.definition: The garbage collector automatically frees memory that your .NET app no longer uses.
topics.why: It prevents memory leaks and reduces the need to manage memory manually.
topics.problem: Without GC, developers would have to free memory manually and risk serious bugs.
topics.realWorldExample: Objects created during request processing are cleaned up after the request ends.
topics.commonMistakes: Forcing garbage collection or holding references too long can hurt performance.

topics.title: Cross-platform .NET Core
topics.content: .NET Core is a cross-platform implementation of .NET that runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
topics.example:
dotnet new console -n MyApp
dotnet run --project MyApp

questions.question: What is .NET Core?
questions.answer: .NET Core is a cross-platform implementation of .NET for building console, web, and cloud apps.

topics.definition: .NET Core is the cross-platform version of .NET for Windows, Linux, and macOS.
topics.why: It lets you build apps that run on different operating systems with the same code.
topics.problem: Without cross-platform support, you would need separate versions of your app for each OS.
topics.realWorldExample: Deploying a web API to a Linux container and a Windows server without changing code.
topics.practicalExample:
dotnet new console -n MyApp
dotnet run --project MyApp
topics.commonMistakes: Assuming file paths or OS behavior are the same on all platforms causes deployment issues.

topics.title: Performance and Deployment
topics.content: .NET Core is optimized for performance and supports lightweight deployment models like self-contained and framework-dependent apps.
topics.example: Publish with dotnet publish -c Release to create distributable app files.

questions.question: How do you publish a .NET Core app?
questions.answer: Use dotnet publish -c Release to create deployable output for your app.

topics.definition: .NET Core performance covers how to make apps fast and efficient.
topics.why: Faster apps use fewer resources and give users a better experience.
topics.problem: Poor performance leads to slow load times and unhappy users.
topics.realWorldExample: Caching database results and using asynchronous I/O in a web app.
topics.practicalExample: Publish with dotnet publish -c Release to create distributable app files.
topics.commonMistakes: Premature optimization or not measuring actual bottlenecks can waste effort.

topics.title: Middleware Architecture
topics.content: Middleware components are software parts assembled into an application pipeline to handle requests and responses. Each component can perform work before and after the next component is called. The order of registration in Program.cs is critical as it dictates the exact sequence in which requests pass through the application.

questions.question: What is ASP.NET Core Middleware?
questions.answer: It is code that is executed in a request/response pipeline. Each component chooses whether to pass requests to the next component.

questions.question: Why does middleware registration order matter?
questions.answer: Because requests flow sequentially. For example, Routing middleware must run before Authorization, which runs before endpoint handlers.

topics.definition: Middleware are pieces of code that run during each HTTP request in an ASP.NET Core app.
topics.why: They let you add logging, authentication, and response handling in a shared pipeline.
topics.problem: Without middleware, request handling becomes harder to reuse and organize.
topics.realWorldExample: Logging every incoming request and then passing control to the next middleware.
topics.commonMistakes: Using middleware in the wrong order or forgetting to call next() blocks requests.

topics.title: Configuration & Options Pattern
topics.content: ASP.NET Core supports multiple configuration providers, loading settings from appsettings.json, environment variables, command-line arguments, and User Secrets. The Options Pattern uses strongly-typed C# classes to represent configuration settings. By registering settings with the `IOptions<T>` interface, you inject values using DI securely.

questions.question: What is the Options Pattern in .NET Core?
questions.answer: A pattern that uses C# classes to bind configuration settings strongly-typed, injecting them into services via dependency injection.

questions.question: What is the difference between IOptions, IOptionsSnapshot, and IOptionsMonitor?
questions.answer: IOptions is a singleton (never changes), IOptionsSnapshot reads settings per-request (scoped), and IOptionsMonitor enables real-time updates.

topics.definition: Configuration in .NET Core reads settings from files, environment variables, and other sources.
topics.why: It keeps environment-specific values separate from application code.
topics.problem: Hardcoding settings makes it difficult to deploy the same app to different environments.
topics.realWorldExample: Reading a database connection string from appsettings.json instead of embedding it in code.
topics.commonMistakes: Storing secrets in source code or mixing config sources inconsistently is risky.

topics.title: Logging & Diagnostics
topics.content: ASP.NET Core has a built-in logging provider (`ILogger`) supporting console, debug, and event log destinations. It supports structured logging (storing parameters instead of just plain string logs), which makes querying logs in tools like Seq or Azure Application Insights incredibly simple. Developers can easily swap the default logger for libraries like Serilog.

questions.question: What is structured logging?
questions.answer: Logging data as key-value property structures rather than simple flat text strings, making logs searchable by parameter values.

questions.question: How can you integrate a third-party logger like Serilog in .NET Core?
questions.answer: By installing the Serilog NuGet package and calling builder.Host.UseSerilog() during application initialization in Program.cs.

topics.definition: Logging records important events and errors from your application.
topics.why: It helps you understand what your app is doing and troubleshoot failures.
topics.problem: Without logs, finding the cause of a production issue can be very difficult.
topics.realWorldExample: Writing an error message when a database query fails.
topics.commonMistakes: Logging too much detail or sensitive data can make logs hard to use and unsafe.

topics.title: Web Request DI Lifetimes
topics.content: In a web application, matching lifetimes with resource scope is vital. DbContext is typically registered as Scoped so that a single database transaction connection is shared throughout the entire duration of a single HTTP request, then disposed when the request concludes. In contrast, Transient resources have no sharing, and Singleton resources are shared globally across all parallel users.

questions.question: Why is DbContext registered as Scoped by default in ASP.NET Core?
questions.answer: To ensure that database queries executed in different parts of a single web request share the same unit of work and connection.

questions.question: What is a transient service used for?
questions.answer: For lightweight, stateless services that perform short independent operations without sharing state across parts of a request.

topics.definition: Web request DI lifetimes control how long injected services live per request, scope, or app.
topics.why: The right lifetime ensures services behave correctly and use memory efficiently.
topics.problem: Using the wrong lifetime can lead to stale data or resource leaks.
topics.realWorldExample: Using scoped services for database contexts and singleton services for shared helpers.
topics.commonMistakes: Using singleton for request-specific services or transient for heavy objects can cause problems.

topics.title: Host & Startup Configuration
topics.content: Modern .NET Core applications combine services configuration and request pipelines in a single file (`Program.cs`) using `WebApplicationBuilder`. The builder manages configuration and registers services to the DI container. Once built, the resulting `WebApplication` instance is used to configure middleware routes, endpoint mappings, and boot the application server.

questions.question: What did WebApplication.CreateBuilder replace in earlier .NET Core versions?
questions.answer: It replaced Startup.cs, consolidating Startup configuration, WebHostBuilder, and Program.cs into a streamlined single-file bootstrap.

questions.question: Where are HTTP routes mapped in modern .NET Core applications?
questions.answer: On the built WebApplication app instance, after builder.Build() is executed.

topics.definition: The host configures and boots an ASP.NET Core application with services and server settings.
topics.why: It sets up the app environment and dependency injection before handling requests.
topics.problem: Without a proper host, the app has no runtime configuration or request pipeline.
topics.realWorldExample: Building a web host that runs Kestrel and configures middleware.
topics.commonMistakes: Altering host settings after the app is built or not adding required services can break startup.

topics.title: API Basics
topics.content: An API is a set of rules that lets different software systems communicate with each other.
topics.example: GET /api/products returns a list of product data in JSON format.

questions.question: What is an API?
questions.answer: An API is an application programming interface that allows applications to talk to each other.

topics.definition: API basics cover how applications communicate over the web using requests and responses.
topics.why: APIs let different systems share data and functionality without a user interface.
topics.problem: Without APIs, integrating services or mobile apps with your backend is difficult.
topics.realWorldExample: A weather app calling an API to get the latest forecast.
topics.practicalExample: GET /api/products returns a list of product data in JSON format.
topics.commonMistakes: Using inconsistent URL patterns or not returning proper status codes causes confusion.

topics.title: RESTful API Design
topics.content: RESTful APIs use HTTP verbs like GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE to manage resources.
topics.example: POST /api/users with user data creates a new user record.

questions.question: What does REST stand for?
questions.answer: REST stands for Representational State Transfer and is a common pattern for designing web APIs.

topics.definition: RESTful API design uses standard HTTP methods and URLs to work with resources cleanly.
topics.why: It makes APIs predictable and easy to use for developers.
topics.problem: Without RESTful principles, APIs become hard to understand and maintain.
topics.realWorldExample: Using GET to read items, POST to create items, PUT to update, and DELETE to remove.
topics.practicalExample: POST /api/users with user data creates a new user record.
topics.commonMistakes: Using POST for every operation or mixing verbs in URLs is not RESTful.

topics.title: ASP.NET Core Controllers
topics.content: Controllers manage HTTP API endpoints by inheriting from `ControllerBase` and applying `[ApiController]` and `[Route]` attributes. Endpoints use action methods decorated with HTTP action attributes (`[HttpGet]`, `[HttpPost]`, etc.) to process incoming parameters and return HTTP status codes via `ActionResult` models.

questions.question: What does the [ApiController] attribute do?
questions.answer: It enables API-specific behaviors like automatic HTTP 400 responses on validation failure, routing requirements, and binding parameter inferences.

questions.question: What is ControllerBase and how is it different from Controller?
questions.answer: ControllerBase has API helper methods. Controller inherits ControllerBase and adds MVC view support, which is unnecessary for Web APIs.

topics.definition: Controllers handle incoming API requests and return responses in ASP.NET Core.
topics.why: They organize endpoints into reusable classes and connect routes to logic.
topics.problem: Without controllers, routing and request handling would be scattered and harder to maintain.
topics.realWorldExample: A ProductsController with actions for list, details, create, update, and delete.
topics.commonMistakes: Putting too much business logic in controllers instead of services makes them hard to test.

topics.title: Minimal APIs
topics.content: Minimal APIs are a lightweight design option in ASP.NET Core. They allow you to create REST endpoints directly in Program.cs with minimal structure, avoiding the boilerplate of controller files. They leverage performance optimizations and are highly recommended for microservices or simple API layouts.

questions.question: What are the benefits of Minimal APIs over Controller-based APIs?
questions.answer: Lower overhead, faster startup performance, simpler structure, and less boilerplate code for microservices.

questions.question: Can you use Dependency Injection with Minimal APIs?
questions.answer: Yes, dependencies can be passed directly as arguments in the route handler function signature.

topics.definition: Minimal APIs let you define endpoints with very little setup in ASP.NET Core.
topics.why: They are faster to write for simple APIs and keep the code small.
topics.problem: Without minimal APIs, small services may need more ceremony to start quickly.
topics.realWorldExample: A quick hello endpoint defined with app.MapGet("/", () => "Hello");
topics.commonMistakes: Using minimal APIs for very complex routes or business logic can make code harder to structure.

topics.title: Content Negotiation & Serialization
topics.content: Content negotiation is the process of selecting the best data representation format for a client. Web API returns JSON by default using System.Text.Json. However, if a client requests XML via the `Accept` request header (`application/xml`), ASP.NET Core can serialize the output to XML if the server has formatters registered in Program.cs.

questions.question: What is Content Negotiation?
questions.answer: The process where the client and server negotiate the format (JSON, XML) of request/response payloads using Accept headers.

questions.question: Which library does ASP.NET Core use for JSON serialization by default?
questions.answer: System.Text.Json, which is built-in and optimized for high performance.

topics.definition: Serialization converts objects to JSON or XML so they can be sent over the network.
topics.why: APIs need a shared data format so clients and servers can understand each other.
topics.problem: Without serialization, data cannot be transferred cleanly between systems.
topics.realWorldExample: Returning a JSON body from an API endpoint with product details.
topics.commonMistakes: Exposing internal fields by default or failing to set the correct content type can cause security and compatibility issues.

topics.title: API Security (JWT & CORS)
topics.content: Securing APIs involves Authentication (identifying who is calling) and Authorization (checking what they can access). Standard Web APIs use JSON Web Tokens (JWT). The API validates the JWT signature on incoming requests. Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) must be configured to specify which web client origins are allowed to interact with the API endpoints.

questions.question: How does JWT Bearer authentication work?
questions.answer: The client sends a token in the Authorization header (Bearer <token>). The server verifies the token signature and extracts user claims.

questions.question: Why is CORS critical for web API developers?
questions.answer: Without CORS configuration, browsers block web clients hosted on different domains from making scripts-based requests to the API.

topics.definition: API security protects endpoints using tokens, CORS rules, and authentication checks.
topics.why: It keeps unauthorized users from accessing private data or actions.
topics.problem: Without security, anyone could call your API and change data or view secrets.
topics.realWorldExample: Using JWT tokens so only logged-in users can call protected routes.
topics.commonMistakes: Allowing all origins in CORS or storing tokens insecurely leaves APIs open to attack.

topics.title: Versioning & Documentation
topics.content: Documenting APIs with Swagger (OpenAPI) allows developers to explore endpoints and test API operations in a browser UI. Versioning is essential to introduce API changes without breaking existing clients. APIs can be versioned via routes (e.g. `/v1/products`), query string parameters (`/products?api-version=1.0`), or HTTP headers.

questions.question: What is Swagger/OpenAPI?
questions.answer: A specification and tool suite (like Swashbuckle) that generates interactive documentation and test clients for Web APIs.

questions.question: What are the common ways to version a Web API?
questions.answer: URL path versioning, Query string parameter versioning, and custom Request Header versioning.

topics.definition: API documentation explains how developers can use your API, including routes and data formats.
topics.why: It makes your API easy to adopt and reduces mistakes from consumers.
topics.problem: Without docs, developers waste time guessing how your API works.
topics.realWorldExample: Swagger UI that shows available endpoints and example requests.
topics.commonMistakes: Leaving docs out of sync with the actual API leads to confusion.
